t: Vector and Cartesian equation of a line
def: A line in 3D can be written vectorially using a point and direction vector, or in Cartesian form using direction ratios.
points: Vector form: r = a + t*b, where a is a point on the line and b is the direction vector.
Cartesian form: (x-x1)/l = (y-y1)/m = (z-z1)/n, using point (x1,y1,z1) and direction ratios l,m,n.
l, m, n in Cartesian form correspond to the components of b in vector form.
To convert vector to Cartesian, write r = xi+yj+zk and equate components.
A line is fully determined by one point on it and its direction.
If two points are given, direction ratios come from subtracting their coordinates.

diagram.draw: Draw a 3D line passing through a labelled point (x1,y1,z1). Draw an arrow alongside showing the direction vector (l,m,n).

example: Line through (1,2,3) with direction (2,-1,4): vector form r=(1,2,3)+t(2,-1,4); Cartesian form (x-1)/2=(y-2)/-1=(z-3)/4.
tip: Always state both forms if asked 'equation of line' generally — some questions expect Cartesian specifically.

t: Equation of a plane (normal, three points)
def: A plane can be defined using a normal vector and a point on it, or using three non-collinear points on the plane.
points: Normal form: n.(r-a) = 0, where n is normal vector and a is a known point on the plane.
Cartesian form from normal: if n=(A,B,C) and point (x1,y1,z1), plane is A(x-x1)+B(y-y1)+C(z-z1)=0.
For three points, find two vectors lying in the plane by subtracting coordinates.
Take cross product of those two vectors to get the normal vector n.
Use any one of the three points with this normal in the point-normal formula.
Three points must not be collinear, otherwise they do not define a unique plane.

diagram.draw: Draw a flat plane. Draw a point A on the plane and an arrow sticking straight out of the plane labelled n (the normal vector).

example: Plane with normal (2,-1,2) through (1,2,3): 2(x-1)-1(y-2)+2(z-3)=0, simplifying to 2x-y+2z-6=0.
tip: When given three points, show the cross-product calculation clearly — this step itself carries marks.

t: Angle between lines, planes, line and plane
def: The angle between two lines uses their direction vectors, between two planes uses their normal vectors, and between a line and a plane uses the direction vector and normal with sine instead of cosine.
points: Angle between two lines with directions b1, b2: cos(theta) = |b1.b2|/(|b1||b2|).
Angle between two planes with normals n1, n2: cos(theta) = |n1.n2|/(|n1||n2|).
Angle between a line (direction b) and a plane (normal n): sin(theta) = |b.n|/(|b||n|).
Note the line-plane angle uses sine, not cosine, because it is measured from the plane, not the normal.
Always take the absolute value so the angle found is acute.
Lines/planes are perpendicular or parallel based on special values of these dot products.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Two directions or normals"] --> B["Compute dot product"]
  B --> C["Divide by magnitudes"]
  C --> D["Lines/planes use cos, line-plane uses sin"]

tip: Remember: line-and-plane angle formula uses SINE, this is the most commonly confused formula in the whole chapter.

t: Distance of a point from a plane
def: The perpendicular distance from a point to a plane is found using the plane's equation and the point's coordinates in a direct formula.
points: Write the plane in the form ax+by+cz+d=0.
Substitute the point's coordinates (x1,y1,z1) into ax1+by1+cz1+d.
Take the absolute value of this result.
Divide by sqrt(a^2+b^2+c^2), the magnitude of the normal vector.
This gives the shortest (perpendicular) distance from point to plane.
If the point lies on the plane, the distance comes out as zero.

diagram.draw: Draw a flat plane and a point P above it. Draw a dashed perpendicular line straight down from P to the plane, labelled d (the distance).

tip: Make sure the plane equation is in the exact form ax+by+cz+d=0 before substituting — rearrange first if needed.

def: Skew lines are lines that do not intersect and are not parallel; the shortest distance between them is found using the cross product of their direction vectors.
points: Write both lines in vector form with points a1, a2 and directions b1, b2.
Compute the cross product b1 x b2.
Compute the vector joining the two points, (a2-a1).
Shortest distance = |(a2-a1).(b1 x b2)| / |b1 x b2|.
If b1 x b2 = 0, the lines are parallel instead of skew, use a different formula.
If the shortest distance is zero, the lines actually intersect.

diagram.draw: Draw two lines in 3D that clearly do not touch or appear parallel (skew). Draw a short perpendicular segment connecting the nearest points of the two lines, labelled d.

tip: Always verify b1 x b2 is not the zero vector first — otherwise this formula does not apply.

def: Two lines in space are coplanar (lie in the same plane) if the scalar triple product of the connecting vector and the two direction vectors equals zero.
points: Take a point on each line, a1 and a2, and find the connecting vector (a2-a1).
Take the direction vectors of both lines, b1 and b2.
Form the scalar triple product [(a2-a1) b1 b2] as a 3x3 determinant.
If this determinant equals zero, the two lines are coplanar.
If coplanar and not parallel, the lines must intersect at exactly one point.
If the determinant is nonzero, the lines are skew (do not lie in one plane).

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Find connecting vector a2-a1"] --> B["Form triple product with b1, b2"]
  B --> C{"Determinant zero"}
  C -->|"yes"| D["Lines coplanar"]
  C -->|"no"| E["Lines skew"]

example: If (a2-a1)=(1,1,0), b1=(1,0,0), b2=(0,1,0): determinant = 0 (since third row/column pattern gives zero in z), so lines are coplanar.
tip: Set up the determinant with rows in order (connecting vector, b1, b2) consistently to avoid sign confusion.
